newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Zaire rebel envoy says ready for talks, wants agenda.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebel envoy says ready for talks, wants agenda.

text.p: A senior official for Zaire's rebels said on Thursday the movement was ready for talks with the government of President Mobutu Sese Seko to end Zaire's civil war but first wanted an agenda for the meeting.
Bizima Karaha, foreign affairs spokesman for rebel leader Laurent Kabila, told BBC radio in Pretoria there were no preconditions for the talks.
Kabila and a small delegation arrived in South Africa on Tuesday as part of attempts by South Africa to get the two warring sides together for face-to-face talks.
Mobutu is represented in South Africa by his nephew and security adviser Honore Ngbanda Nzambo Ko Ayumba, who held talks with President Nelson Mandela earlier on Thursday.

Asked if the rebel delegation met Mobutu's envoy in South Africa, Karaha said: "No, we haven't because we believe that until such time there is an agenda on which we could meet and talk about there is no reason why we should meet.
"Personally, I know that Ngbanda is not my friend and why should I meet him. I can only meet him when he comes to talk to me, not for other reasons," Karaha added.

"We don't have conditions for talks, all that we want is peace. Our movement is fighting for a united democratic, prosperous country where human rights can be respected including the rights of all the minority," he said.
Karaha said he believed the government had a mandate to begin talks.
"The Kinshasa group is so disorganised and there is no coordination between the presidency, the government, the parliament and the army.
"There are representatives from the government and the president's office here and I think for the first time these people will have a full mandate to start serious negotiations," he said.
In Kinshasa, the government said it considered Kabila a puppet but was open to the idea of a regional conference provided all foreign troops left its territory.

"We do not understand how the United States can be pushing us to negotiate with Kabila after recognising that Zaire has been the victim of foreign aggression," Pascale Dema, prime minister Kengo wa Dondo's spokesman, told Reuters.
Zaire has consistently accused neighbouring Rwanda, Uganda and Burundi of invading in support of the Tutsi-led rebels, dismissing Kabila as a pawn in their hands.
Earlier on Thursday Mandela told reporters there had been encouraging progress in his separate talks with the warring parties, but kept the details to himself.
Rebel forces have overrun a 1,000 km (600 mile) stretch of Zaire since they took up arms in October last year.
Ngbanda has said direct talks are part of discussions currently taking place with South Africa and United States officials.
He said Mobutu was committed to a peaceful settlement, but one that must "respect Zaire's territorial sovereignty".
